hero.name: Adidev Panday
hero.intro: I'm a Woodstock School student from Ludhiana, India, headed for aerospace engineering. I build AI-driven apps, publish research, and spend my spare hours watching my interesting Youtube feed, F1, playing the violin, and playing sports. Below, you will find everything that I'm proud of.

about.heading: About Me
paragraphs: I grew up in Ludhiana, Punjab, and study at Woodstock School, taking HL Physics, Math AA, and Computer Science in the IB Diploma. My focus is aerospace engineering where I hope to learn about aerodynamics & propulsion.

Outside class, I love building things. I've shipped many AI-powered web apps, developed a React Native app to tackle teen drunk-driving in my hometown, and published research on the risks of digital trading. I co-founded my school's AI Club, lead the yearbook as Editor in Chief, and used to play first chair violin in the Advanced Orchestra. I've competed in varsity football and basketball, interned in product development and CAD, and served on the Academic Honesty Council (AHC) & NHS.

Personally I feel drawn to problems that reward not just rigor but also creativity: from modeling 4th-down football decisions with game theory for my Extended Essay to studying how a paper plane's wing generates lift for my IA.

research.title: The Rise of Digital Trading: Accessibility Versus Risk of Financial Ruin
research.journal: International Journal of High School Research (IJHSR), Vol. 8, Issue 12
research.pageNote: Paper begins on page 89 of the issue.
research.abstract: Digital trading platforms like Robinhood, Groww, and Zerodha have made market access a few clicks away for anyone, educated or not. This paper examines that double-edged shift, covering gamification, finfluencers, and the real cost of frictionless trading. Digitization is useful, but for financially illiterate users, it is a trapdoor.
research.modalBlurb: You will be redirected to the IJHSR issue PDF. My paper starts on page 89.

research.title: F1 CAR ON A CEILING?
research.abstract: Four documentaries claim an F1 car could drive upside down in a tunnel. None say how fast. This paper builds a ground-effect model of a 2022 to 2025 car and shows the honest answer is not a speed but a window, from 208 km/h where the car can finally hold its own motion, up to 327 km/h where its floor gets dragged into the ceiling.
research.modalBlurb: You will be redirected to f1onceiling.netlify.app, an interactive version of the paper.
research.modalTitle: Open the F1 on a Ceiling paper?

whyAerospace.heading: Why Aerospace?
whyAerospace.subtitle: F1; My Childhood Love
paragraphs: I was three years old in a red toy Formula 1 car before I knew what a car really was, and I have been chasing the same feeling ever since. F1 introduced me to physics: that races are won and lost in how air bends around a machine, that a wing is just an upside-down piece of metal, that seconds are gained and lost through millimeters. This obsession with aerodynamics grew up alongside me.

But aerodynamics is not the full story. Propulsion is what actually currently attracts me to it, ironic right? Thrust perplexes me: how you take stored energy and turn it into controlled, enormous force, how a column of plasma or a breath of burning air can move a body through a sky or past an atmosphere. I think aerodynamics is how a machine survives the unforgiving air but propulsion is how it refuses to be affected by it. That is why I love aerospace.

bullets: Add the most specific course, lab, or professor at {school} that matches propulsion, aerodynamics, or aerospace.
Add the most specific student team, facility, or project at {school} worth naming.

MAE 426 for air-breathing propulsion from first principles, with Prof. Choueiri's EPPDyL next door for Hall thrusters and plasma instabilities. The syllabus I'd build for myself if nobody were grading it.
Princeton Rocketry's Team Orbital, 2027 TigerCub launch. I want my face on princetonrocketry.com/members, standing beside Talon Flores (MAE '28) when the thing goes up.
I built airflowns.netlify.app to solve 2D Navier-Stokes in a browser. That's the outside of the car. Prof. Hultmark's high-pressure tunnel is the inside. Both halves of my obsession, same campus.
princeton.pullQuote: I want my face on princetonrocketry.com/members.

bullets: AAE 439 for combustion instability: why pressure oscillations couple with the acoustic modes of hardware, why a chamber tears itself apart or doesn't.

Zucrow Labs, largest academic propulsion facility in the country, on campus, no clearance required. 124 seconds of LOX/methane in the Morpheus hotfire, Mach diamonds in the plume. I've watched that video 14 times.
My Navier-Stokes sim does external airflow. Zucrow does internal, with fire. Same equations, different boundary conditions.
AE 433 and AE 434 for chamber geometry, nozzle expansion ratios, specific impulse, combustion stability margins. The math that decides whether a chamber survives.
Illinois Space Society's Hybrid Propulsion team, 4 kN of paraffin and Nytrox at Willard airport's retired jet-engine testing facility. 20 students, 8 years of development, one engine.
I want to graduate knowing how to build the engine, not just rewatch the hotfire video eleven times on a laptop in Mussoorie.
uiuc.pullQuote: Graduate knowing how to build the engine, not just rewatch the hotfire.

bullets: AOE 4234 for aerospace propulsion systems and AOE 4604 for booster design, fabrication, and operation. Both offered as technical electives in the propulsion track.
PropEL's Mach 7 hypersonic tunnel, obtained from the Russian Academy of Sciences in the mid-90s. 15 seconds of steady flow at high Mach my laptop sim will never reach.
The Hokies are serious about scramjets through the Hy-V project. I'd pay to spend a semester inside that tunnel.
virginia-tech.pullQuote: 15 seconds of flow my laptop sim will never reach.

georgia-tech.opener: Both ends of propulsion, same roof.
bullets: AE 4451 for jet and rocket propulsion in a single course. Clean teaching of both.

The Ben T. Zinn Combustion Lab for gas turbines, air-breathing engines, and chemical rockets. The High-Power Electric Propulsion Lab next door with the largest university vacuum chamber in the nation for plasma thrusters.
I don't want to pick chemical or electric at 18. GT doesn't make me. Both ends of propulsion, same roof, same semester if I want.
georgia-tech.pullQuote: I don't want to pick chemical or electric at 18.

bullets: 16.50 for aerospace propulsion then 16.512 for chemical, liquid-bipropellant, and hybrid rocket propulsion. Taught properly, with the Draper Lab fellowship pipeline two blocks away.
The MIT Rocket Team and the Space Propulsion Lab, with the IAP course on Aerospace Nuclear Power and Propulsion as the thing I'd actually pay for.
Honest reach. But AirflowNS, a published IJHSR paper, and 14 replays of a Purdue hotfire mean I'd show up for the work, not the brand on the sweatshirt.
The S.B. in Mechanical Engineering at SEAS. Navier-Stokes, vorticity, lift, drag. The physics I first met taping wings onto paper planes in Grade 7.
The Harvard Undergraduate Aerospace Collective launched the first Crimson CubeSat and is firing Mojave Sphinx, the Ivy League's first student-led liquid bi-propellant rocket.
No aerospace major. That's the point. I get to build the path, with Government and Economics next to fluid dynamics on the same transcript.

uc-berkeley.opener: A new major at an old powerhouse.
bullets: The new Aerospace Engineering major Berkeley just launched, built on top of a 150-year-old mechanical and fluid mechanics tradition.
Space Technologies at Cal (STAC), the student group doing CubeSats and attitude-control work. Ambitious new program, room for me to help shape what it becomes.

A new major at an old powerhouse. That's the kind of white space I'd want to build in. The ambition of something being decided now, the rigor of a place that's taught these fundamentals for a century.

uc-davis.opener: A UC that calls it aerospace.
bullets: EAE 130A and 130B for aerospace vehicle design. Two full quarters of actually drawing the airplane, not reading about one.
Davis's degree is explicitly called Aerospace Science and Engineering, backed by the department's own aeronautical wind tunnel. Strong in aerodynamics, unsteady flows, and aeroacoustics.
A UC that calls it aerospace, not mechanical-with-a-track. That naming matters more than it sounds. It tells me where the department puts its attention.
MAE 150 for aerospace propulsion, taught across gas turbines, ramjets, scramjets, rockets, and currently detonation engines. One of the broadest propulsion courses in the UC system.
The UCI Combustion Laboratory. Quieter than Zucrow or Zinn Lab, but one of the most-cited combustion research groups in the country.
Detonation engines are the next thing in propulsion. UCI is already running them. That's the kind of early-signal lab I'd want to work in.
MAE 101A, 101B, 101C for fluid mechanics, viscous flows, and compressible flows. The full ladder, no shortcuts.
#1 public MAE department in the US by research citations. Deep benches in CFD, flow control, and hypersonics.
My F1-on-a-ceiling paper lives in the ground-effect regime. UCSD works at hypersonic. Same equations, next regime up. I want the regime up.
MAE 157A for rocket propulsion, MAE 157B for electric propulsion. Both offered. Both taken by students who care.
Prof. Richard Wirz's Plasma and Space Propulsion Laboratory. Hall thrusters, hollow cathodes, the mathematically harder end of thrust.
Chemical propulsion is loud. Plasma is quiet. UCLA studies the quiet one properly, which is where the next decade of propulsion actually lives.
MEng Aerospace Engineering with a full year in industry built into the degree. Not an internship bolted on. A proper year.
Core mechanical engineering first, aerodynamics and propulsion specialisations later. The specialisation gets earned, not handed to you on day one.
A full year on an engineering floor turning CAD into tolerances before I graduate. That's the gap I want closed, and Bath closes it on purpose.

bristol.opener: Aero in the town that built the Concorde.
bullets: MEng Aerospace Engineering with the National Composites Centre on campus. The three course pillars (aerodynamics, dynamics and control, structures and materials) are exactly the three I keep returning to.
Filton, 15 minutes away, is where the Bristol Aeroplane Company built aircraft from 1910. Airbus, Rolls-Royce, GKN, and the last Concorde ever flown are all still there.
Studying aero in the town where the Concorde was built. Hard to argue with the postcode.

manchester.opener: Reynolds did his pipe experiment here.
bullets: MEng Aerospace Engineering with the School of Engineering's deep fluid mechanics heritage. Osborne Reynolds ran his pipe experiment in this university.
Every Reynolds number I've written in a Physics IA started in this building. The equation is literally named after someone whose desk was here.
When you study fluids where the number was named, the math stops feeling abstract. It feels like continuing someone else's unfinished sentence.
The Melbourne Model: a Bachelor of Science first, then a Master of Engineering (Aerospace). Wide before deep, by design.
Prof. Ivan Marusic's Fluid Mechanics Group, world-class on turbulent boundary layers. The exact fluids regime I want to understand.
I'm a violinist who wants to design engines, a builder of AI apps who publishes research. Melbourne lets me stay more than one thing without pretending I was ever only one.
AEROSP 320 for propulsion and 325 for gas dynamics. Both courses heavy, both taught in one of the oldest aerospace departments in the country.
Prof. Alec Gallimore's Plasmadynamics and Electric Propulsion Laboratory (PEPL), builder of the X3 Hall thruster: 100+ kW, developed with NASA, built with human Mars missions in mind.
Michigan builds the thruster NASA will actually use. Not a scaled model. The thruster. That's a different kind of lab to be inside.
MEng Aerospace Engineering with the Advanced Manufacturing Research Centre (AMRC) on campus, built in partnership with Boeing. One of the UK's top five aero and manufacturing programs.
Sheffield teaches the design AND the build. I've done CAD at BAUM and product development at KGOC. The next step is machining and composites.
Design is only half the job of an engineer. Sheffield teaches the half most courses skip over on the way to a theory exam.

southampton.opener: Mitchell's tunnel. F1 teams rent it.
bullets: Southampton's R.J. Mitchell Wind Tunnel. Mitchell designed the Spitfire. F1 teams have rented this tunnel to develop their cars.
The only Russell Group MEng that combines Aeronautics AND Astronautics, with a vacuum chamber on site for spacecraft propulsion testing. Air and space in one degree.
Downforce pulled me into aerospace. Thrust kept me there. Southampton tests both, in the same building. Hard to find anywhere else that does that.
BSc in Mathematical and Computing Sciences for Artificial Intelligence. One rigorous subject taught as a single discipline, not three loosely-related electives.
Milan, a city built on finance, design, and quiet money. The AI I'd study has somewhere to actually land after graduation.
I've already built five AI apps and published research on digital trading in IJHSR. Bocconi is where those two interests stop being separate hobbies and start being a career.

hku-berkeley.opener: A degree built out of two places.
bullets: Two years at HKU for mechanical engineering foundations, two years at UC Berkeley for the new aerospace major. One degree, two institutions, two continents.
Berkeley just launched aerospace on top of its 150-year mechanical tradition. HKU is one of Asia's top MechE departments. The combination is deliberately unusual.
I've spent five years translating between Ludhiana and Woodstock, two schools, two languages, two kitchens. A degree built out of two places is just the version I'd pick on paper too.

nus.opener: Already sat in that lecture hall.
bullets: The Aerospace Engineering specialisation inside NUS Mechanical Engineering. #8 in the world for engineering by QS, with real propulsion and aerodynamics research groups attached.
I've already sat in Prof. Sow Chorng Haur's nanotech lecture at the NUS Science Summer Camp. The campus is familiar, the research culture is familiar.
Asia's fastest-moving research funding, 5 hours from India by flight. I want to study aerospace in the region I'm from, not away from it.

tu-delft.opener: Walk into the tunnel. Watch it hold.
bullets: AE1222 for aerospace design and the full BSc in the only Faculty of Aerospace Engineering in the Netherlands. #4 in the world for aerospace by QS 2024.
Subsonic, supersonic, and hypersonic wind tunnels reaching past Mach 11, a Cessna they fly as a classroom, and a clean room where students build their own satellites.
I derived the lift equation in a Math HL IA. Delft is where I'd walk into the tunnel and watch it hold.

tum.opener: Classroom to test stand, very short walk.
bullets: The Chair of Turbomachinery and Flight Propulsion (LRG) at the TUM aerospace department in Ottobrunn. Specifically the turbine and engine side, where fuel becomes thrust.
Airbus Defence and Space and the engine builder MTU are a few minutes down the road from the lecture hall. The gap between a class and a real engine is unusually small here.
Germany's top-ranked aerospace program, planted inside Germany's aerospace cluster. Close enough to the test stand to hear it fire.
